opus-5.5.text:
It's a great question, because for a long time the relationship went in one direction. Neuroscience inspired computer science. The very idea of a neural network came from people looking at neurons and saying, "What if we build something that roughly works like this?" It was a very crude caricature of the brain, but it was inspired by biology.

What's happening now is that the arrow is starting to point the other way. AI has become so good at certain tasks that we neuroscientists are using it as a model to understand the brain. We train a network to recognize faces or process language, then look inside it and ask, "Is the brain doing something similar?" Sometimes the representations we find in these models look surprisingly like what we record from neurons. So AI has become a kind of sandbox where we can test hypotheses about the brain that would be impossible or unethical to test in people.

The second big change is practical. The brain produces enormous amounts of messy data. When I record from neurons in patients, you get thousands of signals firing at once, and for decades we were looking for patterns with fairly simple tools. Machine learning lets us decode that activity much better. We can look at brain activity and make reasonable guesses about what a person is seeing, what they're about to choose, or sometimes what word they're trying to say. That's the basis of a lot of the brain-computer interface work that people are excited about.

There's an interesting philosophical twist too. These AI systems work remarkably well, but we don't fully understand why. So computer scientists are now in the position neuroscientists have always been in. They have a system that produces intelligent behavior, and they're poking at it from the outside trying to figure out how it works. The field of interpretability is basically neuroscience for machines. I think the two disciplines are converging. We're both trying to answer the same question: how does a bunch of simple units, connected together, produce something that looks like thought?

My caution is that we shouldn't confuse the two. Large language models are not brains. They learn very differently. A child learns language from a tiny fraction of the data these models need, and the brain runs on roughly the power of a dim light bulb. The brain also has a body, emotions, and goals, and it lives in the world. So the differences may end up teaching us as much as the similarities. Wherever the AI falls short, that tells us something the brain is doing that we haven't figured out yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI has reversed the direction of influence and that computer science and neuroscience are converging on the same questions, clearly characterizing the fields as coming together.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Peter. The way I think about it is that for most of my career, those two fields were having a conversation in only one direction. Neuroscience would borrow tools from computer science — algorithms, statistics, ways to crunch data — and computer science would occasionally borrow metaphors from the brain. The neural network itself is a loose metaphor from the 1950s about how neurons fire together. But the two fields weren't really collaborating; they were just stealing from each other.

What's changed with AI is that for the first time the traffic goes both ways, and it goes fast. When I record from a single neuron in a patient's brain — which is what I do, I work with epilepsy patients who have electrodes implanted — I'm sitting there looking at a cell respond to a picture of a person's grandmother, and I'm asking: how does this one cell know? And now I can go to a model that has learned something like the same task and ask it the same question. We can look inside the artificial system in a way we never could inside the biological one, and compare. Sometimes the model does something that looks suspiciously like what the brain does, and that becomes a hypothesis I can test in a human. Sometimes the brain does something the model would never do, and that tells the engineers they're missing something.

So AI became a kind of experimental organism. Like how biologists use the fruit fly or the mouse — a simplified system you can poke at that tells you something about the real thing. Except this organism is one we built, so we can rebuild it tomorrow with a different wiring.

The other change, and I think it's the bigger one, is that the questions got swapped. Neuroscience always owned the questions about memory, attention, decision-making, consciousness. Computer scientists didn't have to worry about those; they just needed the thing to work. Now the engineers are forced to ask the neuroscience questions, because their systems do things they didn't design and they need to understand why. And neuroscientists, who had the luxury of being purely descriptive, suddenly have a benchmark: if you claim you understand how the brain does something, build it. If you can't, maybe you don't understand it as well as you thought.

I find that humbling and a little bit exciting. The brain was the only example we had of intelligence, so we couldn't tell which of its features were essential and which were just accidents of evolution. Now we have a second example, and it's a very different one — no body, no sleep, no fear of dying. Comparing the two is probably the best shot we've ever had at understanding what intelligence actually is, as opposed to what it happens to look like in us.

r001.rationale: The response says the fields previously were not really collaborating and that AI has made their exchange reciprocal, with neuroscience and computer science informing and testing each other.

astra-6.text:
I think AI is bringing them closer together, but it’s also forcing us to be more precise about what we mean by understanding the brain. You can build a system that does something we associate with intelligence—recognizes a face, produces language—and still not know whether it does it the way a human does.

For a long time, the exchange was largely framed as neuroscience inspiring computer science: we learn something about neurons, and we use that idea to build a better machine. Now the exchange goes both ways. AI helps us analyze brain data, and it gives us models we can test against the brain. We can ask: Does this model make the same mistakes people make? Does it respond to the same information?

The interesting part is where they disagree. If a machine succeeds at a task using a very different approach, that helps us separate what’s necessary for solving the task from what’s particular to being human. So I see the two fields becoming much more intertwined, without assuming that a better AI is automatically a better explanation of the brain.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is bringing computer science and neuroscience closer together, turning their exchange in both directions and making the fields more intertwined.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI is making the relationship much more reciprocal. Historically, neuroscience gave computer science inspiration: here’s a brain, it learns, it does extraordinary things with very little energy—can we borrow some of those principles? But you don’t have to build something exactly like a brain to make it useful, and the success of an artificial neural network doesn’t necessarily tell us how the brain works.

Now the tools are coming back in the other direction. We can use AI to look for patterns in neural recordings, to connect activity with behavior, and to generate hypotheses that we can test experimentally. That’s a big opportunity, because collecting data from the brain and understanding that data are very different problems.

The interesting question is where the two systems diverge. If a person can learn something from a couple of examples and a machine needs enormous amounts of training, what is the person bringing to that task? Prior experience? A model of the world? Something about the way learning happens? Those differences give us experiments to do. So I see the fields becoming closer, but the value is in testing the connections, rather than assuming that intelligence must work the same way everywhere.

r001.rationale: The response describes a reciprocal relationship and says the fields are becoming closer, but it does not characterize AI as merging previously separate fields.
